# Part 3: Reproducibility - basic principles

## The 3 R's of robust research

![](Figures/kedron_frazier_3Rs.png){fig-align="center" width="70%"}

Kedron, P.; Frazier, A.E. How to Improve the Reproducibility,
Replicability, and Extensibility of Remote Sensing Research. *Remote
Sens.* 2022, 14, 5471. https://doi.org/10.3390/rs14215471

## SORTEE guidelines for computational reproducibility

- Pick, J. L., B. J. Allen, B. Bachelot, K. R. Bairos-Novak, J. A.
  Brand, B. Class, T. Dallas, P. B. D’Amelio, E. Fenollosa, E.
  Fernández-Juricic, D. G. E. Gomes, et al. (2026). The SORTEE
  guidelines for data and code quality control in ecology and
  evolutionary biology. Peer Community Journal 6:e20.

  - SORTEE: Society for Open, Reliable, and Transparent Ecology and
    Evolutionary Biology

- Standardized guidelines for 'data editors'

## SORTEE's three goals

![](Figures/SORTEE_3_goals.png){fig-align="center" width="90%"}

## SORTEE guidelines

- Stage 1: *Data* must be archived and adhere to FAIR guiding
  principles.
- Stage 2: Archived *data* corresponds with the data reported in the
  manuscript.
- Stage 3: *Code* must be archived and adhere to FAIR guiding
  principles.
- Stage 4: Archived *code* corresponds with the workflow reported in the
  manuscript.
- Stage 5: Archived *code* runs with the archived *data*.
- Stage 6: Results can be computationally reproduced by running the
  archived code

- No folder hierarchy

- "FINAL" naming chaos
- Undocumented, unnamed scripts
- No README to explain any of it
- Afraid to delete anything

## A logical directory structure

```         
project/        # 1 R project per manuscript
├── Data/       # raw, unmodified source data
├── Derived/    # outputs generated by scripts
├── Figures/    # saved plots
├── Sandbox/    # explore without cluttering Scripts/ folder
├── Scripts/    # reproducible code
    └── 00_wrangling.R 
    └── 01_exploratory.R 
    └── 02a_analysis.R 
    └── 02b_analysis.R 
    └── 03_plotting.R 
    └── 04_manuscript.qmd
└── README.md
```

## Structuring a script

::::: columns
::: {.column width="55%"}
- Clear header: purpose, inputs, outputs
- Section labels for navigation
- One or a few related goals per script
- Should run start to finish (or until `stop()`)
- Output of one script is often input of next script
- See online ['R for Data Science'](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/) free
  textbook
:::

![](Figures/Rstudio_nav_pane.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}
:::

# 4b. Data storage using FAIR principles

## FAIR data principles

- **F**indable — clear naming, documented, ideally with a persistent
  identifier (e.g. DOI)
- **A**ccessible — retrievable via standard, open protocols
- **I**nteroperable — Standard formats, open formats over proprietary
- **R**eusable — well-described, with clear license and provenance

## Data dictionaries

- One row per variable
- Name, type, units, description
- Lightweight — a table is enough

![](Figures/data_dictionary.png){fig-align="center" width="100%"}

## Data paper - Facilitating reuse

- Define data scope
- Provide context
- Detailed methods section
- Quality assurance & control
- Technical aspects - file types, data size, and software needed
- Data collectors credited
- The 4th R: Reusability!
  - [15 minute
    YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jR3Xa2Id-fo&t=774s)

- What order do I run things in?
- License
- Generally written in Markdown (a lightweight markup language)

# 4d. Git & GitHub

## 12 ways to use GitHub in research (I)

Braga et al. (2023, *Methods in Ecology and Evolution*) — roughly
beginner to intermediate:

1.  Archiving citable code and data
    - Requires 'minting' a DOI for long-term storage
2.  Storing and sharing a research compendium
    - Version control
3.  Project management
    - Issues, discussions, projects
4.  Project continuity
    - See project development through time
5.  Open scientific discussion
    - [GitHub Community forum](https://github.community/)
6.  Educational materials
    - Workshops, also see the [GitHub
      Classroom](https://classroom.github.com) tool

## 12 ways to use GitHub in research (II)

7.  Writing a manuscript
    - e.g., Literate programming using Quarto
8.  Asynchronous collaborative coding and writing
    - Clone and fork, merge through pull request
9.  Automation
    - Github actions, triggered by events (e.g. push, pull request or at
      specified times)
10. Hosting a website
11. Organizing and managing teams
12. Peer review

## 12 ways to use GitHub in research (III)

![](Figures/github_12_uses.png){fig-align="right" width="80%"}

Braga, P. H. P. et al. (2023). Not just for programmers: How GitHub can
accelerate collaborative and reproducible research in ecology and
evolution. *Methods in Ecology and Evolution*, 14, 1364–1380.

## Why version control?

- Track changes over time
- Recover earlier versions safely
- Transparency in development
- Refactor and delete with confidence

## GitHub vocabulary

- **Version control** — tracking changes to files over time, with the
  ability to go back
- **Fork** — your own copy of someone else's repository, on GitHub
- **Clone** — download a copy of a repository to your computer
- **Branch** — a parallel line of work, isolated from the main version
  until merged
- **Commit** — save a snapshot of your changes, with a message
- **Push** — upload your local commits to GitHub
- **Pull** — download the latest commits from GitHub to your computer
- **Pull request** — ask the original repo's owner to merge your branch
  in

## Collaborating on GitHub: the workflow

1.  **Fork** the repository, on GitHub
2.  **Clone** your fork, to your computer
3.  **Branch** — create a new branch for your change
4.  Edit your files
5.  **Commit** your changes
6.  **Push** your branch to GitHub
7.  Open a **pull request** back to the original repo

## `.gitignore`

- Decide what *shouldn't* be tracked
- Large/raw data, generated outputs, your darkest secrets Useful tips
- Use asterisks to ignore file types (e.g., `*.xlsx`)
- Ignores entire folders AND everything inside it, at any depth (e.g.,
  `Some_folder/`)
  - Use Some_folder/\* combined with `!pattern` to create exceptions
    (e.g., `!Some_folder/keep_me`)

## Hands-on - Linking Github & Rstudio

- Create a GitHub account, if you don't already have one
- Create your first 'Test' repository
- Link it with an RStudio project (or your preferred IDE)
- Pick a few of the ways you'd like to use Github and implement
- Then, apply this to your own project

## Linking R studio and Github

### Step 1: Create Github repository

- Log into your account on the GitHub Website
- Click the green New or + button to create a new repository
- Enter a repository name—it is best to name it exactly the same as your
  RStudio project
- Depending (2a vs 2b): Add a README and .gitignore?
- Click Create repository

## Step 2: Link Github repo with R studio project

### 2a: If creating a new project...

- File -\> New project
- Click 'Version control', 'Git', then paste url from github
- 'Create Project'

### 2b: If R project already exists...

- Locally, open your existing project in RStudio
- Select Tools -\> Project Options -\> Git/SVN
- Change Version control system from None -\> Git, and click 'Yes' to
  initialize a Git repository.
- Then, in terminal...

```{r}
git remote add origin [insert url]
git branch -M main
git push -u origin main
```

## Git vs GitHub

|   | Git | GitHub |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| What it is | Version control software | Website that hosts Git repositories |
| Runs | Locally, on your computer | On GitHub's servers, over the internet |
| Core function | Version control | Store a remote copy, enable collaboration |
| Needs internet? | No | Yes, to push/pull/access |
| Extra features | — | Issues, pull requests, project boards, Actions |
| Alternatives | Mercurial, SVN | GitLab, Bitbucket |
